title: How an RBA Board member weighs the cost of bringing inflation back to target
summary: Renée Fry-McKibbin described a decision in which two policymakers could agree on where inflation should end up and still disagree about the cash rate today. The objective she set out was the midpoint of Australia’s 2–3 per cent inflation target. The difficult choice is how quickly to return there when reducing demand can also cost jobs. She spoke in her personal capacity as a Monetary Policy Board member. Research can test how costly alternative paths might be, but members can still place different weights on those costs, particularly when they fall on different groups.

Graphs 1 and 2 put the trade-off in historical context. Year-ended inflation has averaged around the target band during the inflation-targeting period, but had risen back above it in the latest year. Employment as a share of the population had eased from its recent peak but remained around 64%, high in the history plotted. Neither chart determines how many jobs a particular rate rise would cost. Participation can change the employment ratio, and aggregate inflation can combine a sharp energy shock with pockets of excess domestic demand. The immediate difficulty she identified was precisely that combination of strong spending in some parts of Australia, weakness in others and a large external oil supply shock.

Fry-McKibbin’s example of how to make a decision under those conditions was the May Statement on Monetary Policy. After the Middle East conflict began, staff published a baseline and two adverse scenarios. The relevant comparison is how inflation and employment fare when a policy judged suitable in the baseline meets a more persistent shock. If the costs are concentrated among people with little room to adjust, a seemingly modest difference between central forecasts can conceal an important difference between policies. She cited a community survey in which 70 per cent of Australians identified inflation as their main economic concern. That measures its salience. It cannot tell a policymaker how the same respondents would weigh a specific increase in unemployment.

AI enters the speech on both sides of the policy decision. Four recent staff studies examined household wealth exposed to AI, Australian data-centre investment, international export prices and early labour-market effects. One household can be exposed through its investments, another through its job, while construction spending may compete for resources today even if the new infrastructure raises productivity later. Fry-McKibbin identified these as channels to investigate. She gave no net estimate of their effect on inflation or the cash rate. The studies reflect their authors’ analysis and can differ from other work at the Bank (endnotes 9–11).

One research programme changes what the Board can know before an official statistical release. Bank researchers developed a tool that can search and aggregate information from roughly 22,000 confidential business interactions over 25 years within the RBA’s secure systems. Firms can discuss their next wage round or hiring decision before it appears in a national release. Adding liaison indicators improved model-based nowcasts for variables including wage growth in the research she described. The speech gives no numerical estimate of that improvement, and the interviews are confidential. A market economist using public surveys would need a separate test of whether those surveys share the same lead.

The practical limit she placed on these tools came from the October RBA research conference. Participants from several central banks emphasised the need to explain difficult choices and to account for past decisions without promising precise outcomes. The distribution of inflation and employment outcomes under alternative scenarios is evidence a Board member can use. It still leaves a judgement about the acceptable speed of adjustment when inflation is above target and parts of the economy are already weak.

questions.question: Under which oil scenario does delaying disinflation materially protect employment?
questions.detail: Keep the policy alternatives and initial conditions common across scenarios. Vary the persistence of the oil shock and the size of domestic pass-through. Compare both the time spent above target and cumulative employment losses, including their concentration across industries. A ranking that reverses with a small change in persistence would reveal exactly where judgment enters the choice.

questions.question: Does business liaison improve the wage forecast when assessed only with information available on the day?
questions.detail: Compare a model using published labour data with one adding a contemporaneous liaison indicator, on identical forecast dates. Separate wages already negotiated from planned awards, check performance around labour-market turning points, and score the forecasts against both first releases and subsequent revisions. The reported aggregate improvement leaves open which industries or phases account for the gain.

questions.question: Which sign of labour-market weakness would outweigh a still-high employment ratio?
questions.detail: Graph 2 puts the employment-to-population ratio high in historical context, while the speech describes weakness in parts of Australia. Compare official hours, vacancies and recruitment by industry with energy exposure and participation, using only releases available before each meeting. A decline in hours and hiring across multiple sectors would say more about the employment costs of restraint than a weakening ratio driven by changes in the composition of the population.

questions.question: Which AI exposures matter first for the balance between inflation and employment?
questions.detail: The four staff studies cited in endnotes 10–11 address different channels without producing a common policy estimate. Compare the timing of construction outlays and labour demand with household wealth exposures, export prices and realised productivity. Read the separate staff papers and contemporary official investment and labour data before treating current spending and prospective supply gains as offsetting effects of the same size.
